summary: Defines service tags and DNS procedures that let a mobile node discover servers offering IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services. Because the tags are used with service records and naming-authority pointers, no rigid domain naming convention is needed. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Think of the phone book as a directory for finding helpers. This document says what to look up in it so a moving device can find the right helper without everyone having to name their computers the same way.

subtitle: How a mobile device uses DNS NAPTR and SRV records to find IEEE 802.21 handover servers.

tldr.problem: A mobile node using IEEE 802.21 needs to find servers offering Media Independent Handover services, and servers may host only some of the three service types.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines service tags (MIHIS, MIHES, MIHCS) and a DNS procedure using NAPTR and SRV records, with the starting domain taken from the home domain, DHCP, a search list or a cache.
tldr.outcome: The procedure yields an IP address, port and transport protocol for the wanted service. It is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 5679 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2009 and is updated by RFC 8553. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Three Handover Services to Find
sections.content:
IEEE 802.21 defines three service types that help a device switch between network technologies. In IEEE terms they are called Media Independent Handover (MIH) services: the MIH Information Service (MIHIS), the MIH Event Service (MIHES) and the MIH Command Service (MIHCS).

The RFC expects that a Mobility Server will not necessarily host all three together, so each type has to be discoverable separately. It therefore defines application service tags that allow service location without relying on rigid domain naming conventions.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of helpers: one that gives information, one that reports what is happening, and one that gives orders. They might live in different buildings, so you need to look for each kind on its own.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
A Mobile Node (MN) is the moving device. A Mobility Server is a network node providing IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services. The home domain is the DNS suffix of the operator with which the MN has a subscription, usually stored in the MN as part of the subscription.

An application service is a generic type of application, independent of the protocol used to offer it. An application protocol implements that service. Each has an IANA-registered tag.
sections.eli5: The moving device is the traveler, the server is the helper, and the home domain is the name of the company the traveler pays to belong to.

sections.title: Where Discovery Starts
sections.content:
The procedure builds on the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS), which maps a string to data by repeatedly applying rewrite rules stored in DNS as NAPTR records. Existing DDDS applications treat the First Well Known Rule as fixed. This RFC makes its input dynamic, based on the search path the resolver discovers or is configured with.

For the home domain, the input to the First Well Known Rule MUST be the MN's pre-configured home domain. For a local (visited) domain, the MN SHOULD use DHCP as described in RFC 5678 to find the address of the server and contact it directly. If neither an address nor a domain name results, the MN MAY request a domain search list and use it as input. It may also use unexpired cached domain names learned from an earlier MIH Information Service query.

If no valid domain names are found, the MN MUST stop trying to discover MIH services. The dynamic rule SHOULD NOT be used for other services unless a future specification says so.
sections.eli5: First you decide which phone book to open: your home company's, or one you are told about when you arrive. If you cannot find any phone book, you stop looking.

sections.title: Choosing a Service
sections.content:
The MN picks the service it needs. The identifiers are MIHIS, MIHES and MIHCS for the Information, Event and Command Services.

A server supporting any of these services MUST support at least UDP and TCP as transport, as described in RFC 5677. SCTP and other transports MAY also be supported.
sections.eli5: You choose which helper you want by its name tag. Every helper must be reachable by at least two kinds of messenger.

sections.title: Choosing a Transport with NAPTR
sections.content:
The client then selects a transport. The NAPTR service field has the form ID+M2X, where ID is the service identifier and X is a letter for a transport: M2U for UDP, M2T for TCP and M2S for SCTP.

Each NAPTR record points to the SRV record for that transport. The record MUST have an empty regular expression and a replacement value naming the domain where the SRV record lives. The MN MUST discard service fields that are not M2X for transports it supports. NAPTR processing per RFC 3403 then yields the server's most preferred transport that the client supports.

If no NAPTR records are found, the client builds SRV queries for each transport it supports, using _MIHIS, _MIHES or _MIHCS. A client already configured with a transport can query SRV directly, for example _MIHIS._tcp.example.com. The regexp field MUST NOT be used, because it can be complex and error prone and the static target is enough.
sections.eli5: The phone book lists each helper with the ways you can reach them, in order of preference. You pick the best way that your own device also understands.

sections.title: From SRV Record to Address and Port
sections.content:
The port number comes from the Port field of the SRV answer. The TARGET field is a fully qualified domain name that MUST have one or more address records, and it MUST NOT be an alias: there must be no CNAME or DNAME at that name.

Unless the SRV response already carried enough address records in the Additional Data section, the MN performs A and/or AAAA lookups. The result is a list of IP addresses, each usable with the transport chosen earlier.
sections.eli5: The last step is turning the helper's name into a street address and a door number, so your device knows exactly where to knock.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA maintains a table mapping NAPTR service field values to transport protocols. A registration must give the service field, the protocol (name, acronym and a reference document), and the registrant's contact details.

Nine values were placed in the registry: MIHIS, MIHES and MIHCS, each with +M2T (TCP), +M2U (UDP) and +M2S (SCTP). New service fields and new transports for existing fields require Standards Action. IANA was also asked to register MIHIS, MIHES and MIHCS as service names in the Protocol and Service Names registry.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of the name tags and what messenger each one means, so everyone spells them the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to known threats to DNS-based services and says DNSSEC protects against most of them, so deployers are recommended to consider DNSSEC and its operational practices. Where DNSSEC is not feasible, measures should be taken against forged DNS responses and cache poisoning.

If inputs arrive through DHCP, DHCP weaknesses also matter: being unable to authenticate DHCP discovery results can make the mobility service results wrong even if the DNS process was secured.
sections.eli5: If someone swaps the phone book or lies about which book to open, you could be sent to the wrong helper. Signed phone books help, but the instruction about which book to use must be trustworthy too.
